target: Eu tô precisando de um café.
tip: Tô is casual shorthand for estou: Eu tô precisando = I'm needing. You write estou but say tô.

target: Eu gosto muito de praia.
tip: 'Gostar de' always requires the preposition 'de.' You can't say 'gosto praia' – it must be 'gosto de praia.'

target: A comida está salgada demais.
tip: Demais after an adjective means too or excessively: salgada demais = too salty. It follows the word it intensifies.

target: Ainda bem que deu certo.
tip: 'Ainda bem' is literally still well and works as thank goodness, so 'Ainda bem que deu certo' expresses relief.

target: Ela gosta muito do trabalho dela.
tip: When 'gostar de' is followed by a definite article, contractions happen: gostar do (de + o), gostar da (de + a), gostar dos/das.

target: Ela é loira de olhos azuis.
tip: 'De olhos azuis' is how you describe eye color in Portuguese – literally 'of blue eyes.' Same pattern for hair: de cabelos pretos.

target: Com licença, onde fica o banheiro?
tip: 'Com licença' is used when you need to get past someone or interrupt politely. It's more common than 'desculpe' for these situations.

target: Nós preferimos ir de carro.
english: We prefer to go by car.
tip: 'Preferir' = to prefer. Unlike 'gostar' and 'precisar,' it does not take 'de': 'preferimos ir' (not 'de ir').

target: Que saco, perdi o ônibus!
english: How annoying, I missed the bus!
tip: Perder means to miss transport, not just to lose: perdi o ônibus = I missed the bus.

target: Pois não? Em que posso ajudar?
english: Of course? How can I help you?
tip: 'Pois não' is a formal/polite way to say 'how can I help you.' You'll hear it from shopkeepers, receptionists, and servers.

target: A gente gosta de viajar no Carnaval.
english: We like to travel during Carnival.
tip: 'A gente' means we but takes third-person singular, so it is 'a gente gosta', never gostamos.

target: Ela gosta de ler antes de dormir.
english: She likes to read before bed.
tip: After 'de' Portuguese uses the plain infinitive where English uses -ing, so 'gosta de ler' means likes reading.

target: A minha cachorra é pequena e branca.
english: My dog is small and white.
tip: Colors agree with gender and number: branco/branca/brancos/brancas. Some colors don't change: laranja, rosa, violeta.

target: Eu vi ela no supermercado ontem.
english: I saw her at the supermarket yesterday.
tip: 'Ver' past: eu vi. 'Vi ela' is informal; formal would be 'a vi.' But 'vi ela' is standard in speech.

target: Ela quis saber todos os detalhes.
english: She wanted to know all the details.
tip: Quis is the irregular past of querer (to want): eu quis, ela quis. The stem becomes quis, with no accent.

target: Ela é muito parecida com a mãe.
english: She looks a lot like her mom.
tip: Parecido takes com, not a: parecida com a mãe = looks like her mom. Use com for resemblance.

target: A gente pôde sair mais cedo ontem.
english: We were able to leave early yesterday.
tip: The circumflex is the only difference between 'pôde' (was able, past) and 'pode' (can, present), so watch the accent.

target: Ele fez uma piada e todo mundo riu.
english: He told a joke and everyone laughed.
tip: 'Todo mundo' means everyone but is grammatically singular: 'todo mundo riu' = everyone laughed.

target: Já volto, espera um minutinho.
english: I'll be right back, wait just a minute.
tip: The diminutive '-inho' softens requests. 'Um minutinho' (a little minute) sounds much more polite than 'um minuto.'

target: Ela é a profissional mais qualificada da equipe.
english: She's the most qualified professional on the team.
tip: For the superlative, add a definite article before mais: a mais qualificada = the most qualified.

target: Nada a ver, não foi isso que eu disse.
english: That has nothing to do with it; that's not what I said.
tip: 'Nada a ver' is literally nothing to see, but it means nothing to do with it, a common way to reject a claim.

target: Valeu, cara!
tip: 'Valeu' is the most casual way to say 'thanks' in Brazil. It literally comes from 'valer' (to be worth). Very informal but used everywhere.

target: De jeito nenhum!
tip: 'Nenhum/nenhuma' (none/not any) – stronger than simple 'não', emphasizing complete absence.

target: É pra já!
tip: 'Pra' is the everyday spoken contraction of 'para' (for/to). 'É pra já' literally 'it's for now', meaning right away.

target: Se cuida, viu?
tip: 'Viu' (literally 'did you see') is added at the end of sentences as a tag question meaning 'okay?' or 'got it?'. Very Brazilian.

target: Tá bom, eu concordo.
tip: 'Tá bom' is the casual contraction of 'está bom' – used constantly to mean 'okay/alright.' Also: 'tá' for 'está,' 'tô' for 'estou.'

target: E aí, tudo certo?
tip: 'E aí' is a very casual greeting, like 'hey' or 'what's up.' Often followed by 'tudo bem?' or 'tudo certo?'

target: Nossa, que calor!
tip: 'Nossa' (short for 'Nossa Senhora' = Our Lady) is the most common exclamation in Brazil. Used for surprise, shock, or emphasis.

target: Que demora, hein!
tip: 'Que' + a noun makes an exclamation: 'Que demora' = what a delay. No article is needed after 'que' here.

target: Tô atrasado, vou correndo!
tip: 'Ir' + gerund shows an action underway: 'vou correndo' = I'm off running/rushing, not a plain future tense.
